passages.text: Multiplexed isobaric quantitative cross-linking reveals drug-induced interactome changes in breast cancer cells

The study of protein structures and interactions is critical to understand their function. Chemical cross-linking of proteins with mass spectrometry (XL-MS) is a rapidly developing structural biology technique able to provide valuable insight into protein conformations and interactions, even as they exist within their native cellular environment. Quantitative analysis of cross-links can reveal protein conformational and interaction changes that occur as a result of altered biological states, environmental conditions, or pharmacological perturbations. Our laboratory recently developed an isobaric quantitative Protein Interaction Reporter (iqPIR) cross-linking strategy for comparative interactome studies. This strategy relies on isotope encoded chemical cross-linkers that have the same molecular mass, yet produce unique and specific isotope signatures upon fragmentation in the mass spectrometer which can be used for quantitative analysis of cross-linked peptides. The initial set of iqPIR molecules allowed for binary comparisons. Here, we describe the in vivo application of an extended set of six iqPIR reagents (6-plex iqPIR) allowing multiplexed quantitative interactome analysis of up to six biological samples in a single LC-MS acquisition. Multiplexed iqPIR is demonstrated on MCF-7 breast cancer cells treated with five different Hsp90 inhibitors revealing large scale protein conformational and interaction changes specific to the molecular class of the inhibitors.
Graphical Abstract
INTRODUCTION

The plasticity of protein conformations and interactions enable the myriad of biological functions necessary for life. Therefore, analytical techniques capable of probing protein structures and interactions as they exist within cells under a variety of conditions, are critically important to improved understanding of biological systems. The most widely employed structural biology techniques, including X-ray crystallography, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), generally require large amounts of highly purified proteins, and provide extremely detailed, yet static snapshots of protein structures and interactions. Chemical cross-linking with mass spectrometry (XL-MS) is a rapidly developing analytical technique which provides low resolution, yet large-scale structural information on proteins and protein complexes in the form of distance restraints between cross-linked amino acid residues. Importantly, since the cross-linking reaction can occur within cells, identified cross-linked sites can be informative of the ensemble of conformations and interactions present during the reaction period. Subsequent purification of cross-linked proteins and peptides followed by MS analysis and identification of the cross-linked sites provides insight into protein structures and interactions as they exist within cells.

Integration of quantitative MS strategies with XL-MS allows for investigation into the structural dynamics of proteins and protein complexes in complex systems under varying biological states such as disease versus healthy control, altered growth or environmental conditions, and drug treatment. The majority of quantitative XL-MS (qXL-MS) strategies explored to date have utilized the incorporation of stable heavy isotopes, either by metabolic incorporation of isotopes into proteins (i.e., SILAC), or use of isotopically light and heavy cross-linker molecules. Generally, the aforementioned strategies allow for binary comparisons to be made and rely on quantitation by extraction of the MS1 chromatographic signal from light and heavy cross-linked peptides. While SILAC based qXL-MS has successfully been applied to compare drug resistant and sensitive cell lines as well as the dose dependent response of chemotherapeutic agents, the limitation of binary comparisons makes these studies labor intensive, requiring separate LC-MS analyses for each comparison. Furthermore, despite reversed-phase LC separation the MS1 signal at any given time can be quite complex with contributing ions from many different species which can complicate peak detection and quantitation. Additionally, light and heavy cross-linkers have typically used deuterium as the heavy isotope which produces a retention time shift between isotope partners. Traditional quantitative proteomics has, for many years now, relied on isobaric chemical tag labeling (i.e., iTRAQ and TMT) to allow multiplexed quantitative analysis based on isotope encoded reporter ions present in tandem mass spectra of labeled peptides. In 2016, Yu et al. demonstrated the QMIX approach, combining TMT labeling with DSSO cross-linking . QMIX requires a second chemical labeling reaction after the cross-linking reaction and enzymatic digestion to apply the isobaric tags which can result in greater variability in product level formation.

To overcome some of these issues we recently developed a qXL-MS strategy termed isobaric quantitative Protein Interaction Reporter (iqPIR). The iqPIR technology relies on chemical cross-linkers that have heavy isotopes (13C and 15N) incorporated into specific locations within the molecular structures of the cross-linkers such that a set of iqPIR reagents have exactly the same molecular mass yet produce distinct quantifiable isotope patterns upon fragmentation within the mass spectrometer. While initially demonstrated with a binary set of iqPIR reagents, the concept is extensible to allow for multiplexed quantitative comparisons. The accompanying manuscript describes the design and synthesis of a set of six iqPIR cross-linker molecules (6-plex iqPIR) allowing for multiplexed analysis of up to six biological samples within a single LC-MS acquisition. With the synthesis of the multiplexed iqPIR cross-linkers, we evaluated their performance using defined multiplexed samples consisting of purified cross-linked proteins mixed at defined ratios, for which it was found that the multiplex iqPIR approach could accurately reflect the relative abundances of cross-linked proteins in the samples. Here, we address the performance of the multiplex iqPIR approach on complex biological samples, namely breast cancer cells (MCF-7), which have been treated with 5 different heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) inhibitors, with 3 different replicates. Specifically, three drugs targeted the Hsp90 N-terminal domain (17-AAG, XL-888, and ganetespib), one the middle domain (gambogic acid), and the last the C-terminal domain (novobiocin). All treatments were compared to an untreated control (Figure 1). The results presented here demonstrate that multiplexed iqPIR allows for quantitative comparison of large-scale drug induced protein conformational and interaction changes within living cells. We find here that iqPIR derived quantitation is reflective of the class of inhibitor. The data show that within a single tandem mass spectrum, quantitation of the iqPIR encoded isotope patterns allows for comparison of cross-linked peptides originating from six different cross-linked MCF-7 cell preparations. Globally, the results presented here demonstrate that the multiplexed iqPIR strategy simplifies sample preparation and analysis of in vivo cross-linked samples, saving LC-MS analysis time while generating reproducible quantitative data for a large fraction of identified cross-links in multiplexed samples. We envision the approach presented here to be an important advancement for future qXL-MS investigations into the interactome of complex biological systems.
METHODS
Cell culture and harvesting
MCF-7 cells were treated with different concentrations of Hsp90 inhibitors. Complete information on drug treatment and IC50 measurements is made available in Supporting Information.
In vivo 6-plex iqPIR cross-linking

In vivo randomized cross-linking of six biological samples of MCF-7 cells with 3 replicates is described in Supporting Information. Information on the synthesis and molecular details of the 6-plex iqPIR cross-linkers is made available in the accompanying manuscript by Chavez et al. .
Sample preparation
Six independent cross-linked cell pellets were prepared as previously described and merged into a multiplexed sample. Complete information is available in Supporting Information.
LC-MS/MS analysis of cross-linked peptides
LC-MS/MS was performed as previously described and complete information is made available in Supporting Information.
Data analysis
In silico analysis of the 6-plex iqPIR qXL-MS data was done as described by Chavez et al. . Further details are made available in Supporting Information.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

The ability to probe protein structures and interactions from within their native cellular environment in an untargeted fashion and on a systems-wide scale will serve as an important tool in structural and systems biology research. Here, we demonstrate the 6-plex iqPIR qXL-MS strategy in vivo on six biological samples of breast cancer cells (MCF-7; Figure S1), with 3 different replicates, treated with 5 different Hsp90 inhibitors and a vehicle control, to assess large-scale drug induced changes in protein conformations and interactions. The specific Hsp90 inhibitors used here were chosen as they bind to different domains of the same primary protein target and are therefore useful for demonstrating drug class specific protein conformational and interaction changes. Specifically, we chose the canonical Hsp90 inhibitors targeting the ATP binding pocket in the N-terminal domain (NTD; 17-AAG, XL-888, and ganetespib), gambogic acid which binds to the middle domain (MD) of Hsp90, and the C-terminal domain (CTD)-binding novobiocin. This strategy allowed the labeling of six different cell conditions, including untreated control, multiplexed in one final sample before the proteolytic digestion and further sample preparation and LC-MS analysis. Multiplexing samples has several benefits including requiring less starting material from each condition, streamlining sample preparation, minimizing unintended variance, reducing LC-MS analysis time and ultimately simplifying data analysis. Generation of 6-plex iqPIR qXL-MS data required that we develop new computational strategies for automated analysis of the data, which are described in detail in the accompanying manuscript. After in silico analysis, a total of 2,576 non-redundant cross-links were identified for the combined 3 replicates, with estimated 1% FDR, with 42% inter-links (inter-protein links), corresponding to 2,094 site pairs and 622 protein pairs. The complete cross-linking information for the 3 replicates analyzed separately and for the combined data is made available in Figures S2–4, Table S3, and online at http://xlinkdb.gs.washington.edu/xlinkdb/MCF-7_6plex_Bruce.php. In addition to computing drug treatment cross-link log2 ratios independently for reach replicate (Table S3), they were also calculated from the combined quantified ions of all three replicates. We note that having multiple quantitative signals from each iqPIR channel present in each assigned mass spectrum results in high quantitative coverage of the data. For instance, 92.5% of all cross-links (2,379 out of 2,576 total) were quantified and had log2 ratios (i.e., each drug treatment versus the untreated control) assigned throughout the five drug treatments. The 95% confidence intervals of the combined drug treatment log2 ratios thereby reflect the reproducibility of the quantitation among the contributing replicates. Indeed, the multiplexed iqPIR data displayed reproducible quantitative results with 1,767 (69%) of the cross-links quantified across all six channels, with 95% confidence intervals no greater than log2 1. Moreover, approximately 40% of the cross-linked peptides have log2 ratios ranging from −0.5 to 0.5 across different preparations. This can be considered the range of non-changing links containing all experimental and biological variability. This demonstrates that reproducibility was observed across six different biological samples within a single multiplexed sample as a significant number of cross-links (723 out of 1,767) have ratios that do not change between the different preparations. In fact, with 6 biological replicates in HeLa 6-plex sample over 90% of the log2 ratios with 95% confidence intervals less than 1 fall within the range of −0.5 to 0.5, with similar variance throughout the 15 ratios (Figure S5a&c). Examining the same unchanging range in the MCF-7 dataset demonstrates the unchanging cross-links have a similar variance throughout the 5 ratios (treatment compared to control), based on the standard deviations (Figure S5b&d). Figure S5e shows the low variability among log2 ratios of housekeeping keratins KRT8 and KRT18 in HeLa 6-plex and MCF-7 6-plex samples. Cross-links with log2ratios outside of this range (log2 −0.5 to 0.5) quantified with 95% confidence intervals of less than 1 are changing due to effects of the drug treatments. Additionally, we examined the quantitative reproducibility of cross-links having distinct masses, which span the same residue pairs as they represent independent measurements of the same structural features (Figure S6), and over 90% of log2 ratios varied below log2 0.2 within cross-linked peptide groups with methionine oxidation or missed cleavages, throughout the 6 channels.

The iqPIR approach can also be used to measure protein level abundance changes by quantifying dead-end cross-links, where one reactive group of the cross-linker reacts with water and the other with a reactive residue site within a protein, in combination with intra-protein cross-links, as was previously demonstrated. Here, a total of 2,092 dead-ends and intra-links combined were quantified throughout the 6 samples, with zero missing values and 95% confidence intervals for the log2 ratios less ≤ 1, which provides relative protein level log2 ratios for 282 proteins. Specifically, from 1,767 cross-links quantified across all six channels, with zero missing values and having 95% confidence intervals for the log2 ratios ≤ 1, 1,492 cross-linked peptides had protein quantitation assigned with the same parameters (zero missing values and having 95% confidence intervals for the log2 ratios ≤ 1), corresponding to 264 proteins with cross-linked peptides. Having both protein level and cross-link level quantitative values allows for distinguishing conformational and protein interaction level changes from protein abundance level changes.

Globally, the cross-links displayed distinct quantitative patterns in each of the 6 iqPIR channels. To evaluate the data for drug specific information, we compared data across the five different drug treatments using a set of confidently quantified cross-links (95% confidence interval for log2 ratio ≤ 1). Hierarchical clustering of the cross-link ratios using an average pairwise Euclidean distance indicates a high degree of similarity among cross-link ratios of NTD binding drugs (17-AAG, XL-888, and ganetespib), which cluster separately from gambogic acid and novobiocin ratios – MD and CTD binding inhibitors, respectively (Figure 2a). The high level of agreement in quantitative values across the three biological samples treated with NTD binding drugs demonstrates that reproducibility is achievable with the multiplexed iqPIR approach for in vivo cross-linked samples. Differences in the quantitative profiles of cross-link ratios exist despite the fact that the global distribution of cross-link ratios from the different drug treatments display a large degree of overlap (Figure 2c). While all distributions in Figure 2c are centered near a log2 ratio of zero, the distributions of novobiocin and gambogic acid are overall wider than that of the other drugs. The overlap of non-changing ratios across the 6 biological samples indicates reproducibility in the quantitative measurements as it is reflective of background variability. Quantitative changes beyond this are able to be clearly distinguished and are evident based on the quantitative data clustering according to the primary domain target of the drugs. Furthermore, linear correlation analysis of cross-link ratios between drug classes revealed higher correlation and measured coefficients of determination (R2) between NTD targeting drugs when compared with MD-binding gambogic acid and CTD-binding novobiocin (Figure 2b). Thus on a global level drug class specific information was revealed within the large-scale qXL-MS data.

After assessing large-scale changes on MCF-7 cross-links with drug treatments using the 6-plex iqPIR cross-linking, we further investigated specific changes involving Hsp90, the primary target for the inhibitors used here (Figure 3). Hsp90 is a cytosolic heat shock protein with two different isoforms: the inducible Hsp90α and the constitutively expressed Hsp90β. Specifically, a total of 61 cross-links were identified for Hsp90α/β, with 23% inter-links, corresponding to 46 site pairs. Forty-four cross-link pairs had log2 ratios assigned for all 5 drug treatments (zero missing ratio values), within the 95% confidence interval threshold ≤ 1. Due to the homology and sequence similarity between Hsp90α and Hsp90β (Figure S7), the two proteins have corresponding lysine residues that were found cross-linked in this study (Table 1). Comparison of the subset of Hsp90 cross-links reveals more distinguishing quantitative profiles highlighting the similarity of the NTD inhibitors, distinct from MD inhibitor gambogic acid and CTD inhibitor novobiocin (Figure 3a,c&d). Specifically, Hsp90-related cross-link ratios resulting from novobiocin treatment are mostly not changing, while those from gambogic acid and NTD inhibitors are either increasing or display no change. Evaluating the Hsp90 isoform specific information in more detail revealed that, after treatment with inhibitors that bind to the NTD, cross-link log2 ratios are mainly increasing for Hsp90α homodimers (Figure 3c). This is an expected result based on induction of Hsp90α abundance and the general heat shock response induced by NTD inhibitors. Overall, these multiplexed iqPIR qXL-MS results agree with previous SILAC-based qXL-MS findings on HeLa cells treated with NTD-binding drugs 17-AAG and XL-888, and CTD-binding novobiocin. One example is the Hsp90β/α heterodimer (FYEAFSK435NLK_FYEQFSK443NIK), which has increasing ratios after treatment with NTD-binding drugs and gambogic acid, but decreasing log2 ratio after novobiocin treatment (Figure 3c). As the CTD is important in dimerization of Hsp90 (Figure 3b), this observation is consistent with previous reports that CTD inhibitors disrupt Hsp90 dimerization. The lysine residues K435 and K443 are located in the middle domain of Hsp90β and α, respectively (Figure 3b&c). The binding of 17-AAG, XL-888, and ganetespib to the ATP pocket located within the NTD of Hsp90α leads to increased Hsp90α homodimer levels, agreeing with the results found here.

The MS1 and MS2 spectra for the Hsp90β_Hsp90α heterodimer (cross-linked peptides FYEAFSK435NLK_FYEQFSK443NIK) are shown in Figure 4. The MS1 spectrum shows the isotope envelope of the precursor ion, comprised of all 6 isobaric cross-linked peptide ions. MS2 spectrum reveals fragments ions, including the released reporter ions, released intact peptide A/B (FYEAFSK435NLK_FYEQFSK443NIK) ions, and backbone y-type and b-type fragment ions from peptides A/B. The observed isotope encoded peaks from released peptide and backbone fragment ions from each channel are used for cross-link quantitation (Figure 4b&d). Due to signal overlap resultant from the isotope spacing between the iqPIR channels 2 Da (or 1 Da between 818 and 816 channels) the observed iqPIR isotope envelope requires deconvolution of the signal into the six channels. This is accomplished using information on natural isotope abundances as described in detail in the accompanying manuscript by Chavez et al. . Reporter ion signal is not used for quantitation due to ratio compression effects resultant from co-isolation of multiple precursor ions, as observed previously. Since there is no full length structural model of human Hsp90α in the PDB, the Hsp90β K435_K443 Hsp90β/α heterodimer is represented on a homologous Hsp90β structure (PBD 5FWK; Figure 4c). Overall, the cross-linking results obtained here with in vivo application of 6-plex iqPIR technologies to MCF-7 cells demonstrate the first large-scale quantitative cellular interactome changes observed with multiple drugs.

Although the three NTD-binding inhibitors had similar effects on Hsp90 cross-link ratios as expected (Figure 3), multiple cross-link ratios for the ADP/ATP translocase 2 are decreasing after treatment with gambogic acid (MD-binding), ganetespib and XL-888 (NTD binding), differing from 17-AAG (NTD-binding) ratios, which remain unaltered with treatment (Figure 5). Thus, multiplex cross-linking results can highlight similarities across different drug classes as well. ADP/ATP translocase 2 (ADT2_HUMAN) is a mitochondrial transporter of ADP and ATP existing in two states: the mitochondrial matrix-open m-state and the cytoplasm-open c-state. The Jwalk Solvent Accessible Surface Distance (SASD) calculations between cross-linked lysines reveal that the cross-link between lysine residues K272_K23 (AFFK272GAWSNVLR_DFLAGGVAAAISK23TAVAPIER) is only compatible with the m-state (31.43 Å compared with 66.61 Å of c-state; Figure 5a). We note that the lysine residue K23 is embedded in the ATP-binding site of ADT2. The difference in distances between the two states along with decreasing ratios of the K272_K23 link in the m-state suggests that treatment with XL-888, ganetespib, and gambogic acid decreases m-state levels and shifts ADT2 conformational equilibrium towards the c-state. This could potentially result from the binding of ATP-mimetic XL-888 and ganetespib to the ATP-binding pocket of ADT2 in the intermembrane space, interrupting the transport of ATP by the m-state and shifting the protein equilibrium to the ADP-bound c-state. Accordingly, it has been previously reported a loss of mitochondrial membrane potential after treatment of vemurafenib resistance cell lines with XL-888. Evidence shows that ganetespib induces apoptosis in MCF-7 cells by mitochondria-mediated pathways of cell death. Gambogic acid induced mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization in MCF-7 cells, disrupting the ATP transport. On the other hand, no change in K272_K23 cross-link level was observed after treatment with 17-AAG (Figure 5b; log2 ratio between −0.5 and 0.5), which is also an ADP mimetic. These results illustrate how the 6-plex qXL-MS information can reveal unexpected patterns in protein conformations other than the primary drug target.

Moreover, Figure 5b & S8 show the 6-plex iqPIR dead-end-based estimation of ADT2 abundance in the samples after treatment with Hsp90 inhibitors. Many of the cross-links involving ADT2 display similar quantitative values as the protein abundance level changes, indicating that the inhibitors gambogic acid and ganetespib resulted in decreased protein levels for ADT2. However, the inhibitors novobiocin, XL-888, and 17-AAG did not alter ADT2 levels. Cross-linked peptides K147_K272 and K94_K23 display quantitative values that differ from the protein abundance levels, thus indicative of conformational changes. The protein abundance information is available on the cross-linking interaction table online at http://xlinkdb.gs.washington.edu/xlinkdb/MCF-7_6plex_Bruce.php.
CONCLUSION

Here we have presented the application of a new multiplexed iqPIR qXL-MS strategy for probing protein conformational and interaction changes in MCF-7 cells treated with 5 different Hsp90 inhibitors, with 3 different replicates. The results demonstrate that quantitative comparison of relative cross-linked peptide abundance levels from up to 6 separate multiplexed biological samples is possible using the isotope encoded fragment ion intensities present in iqPIR cross-linked peptide MS2 spectra. On a global level, the quantitative results reflect the various classes of Hsp90 inhibitors with the three NTD targeting drugs (17-AAG, XL-888, and ganetespib) displaying highly similar quantitative profile patterns while the inhibitors targeting the MD (gambogic acid) and CTD (novobiocin) display distinctive profiles. The results from this study demonstrate that the technique can provide accurate quantitative information on samples with changing protein abundance levels, changing protein conformations and interaction levels and can be applied on large-scale in vivo qXL-MS studies. Quantitative profiles of cross-links within Hsp90α and Hsp90β matched those expected with NTD inhibitors as previously observed from a study employing SILAC based qXL-MS using HeLa cells. The data in this manuscript contain quantitative information from MCF-7 cells revealing the response of hundreds of protein pairs to different Hsp90 inhibitors. The application of multiplexed iqPIR strategy presented here, together with advanced features described in the accompanying manuscript, illustrates a significant advancement for qXL-MS, simplifying sample preparation, saving LC-MS acquisition time, and allowing for comparison of up to 6 biological samples from a single LC-MS acquisition.

6-plex iqPIR experimental workflow.

(a) MCF-7 cells were treated with 5 different Hsp90 inhibitors. Treated cells were separated in 3 different replicates and cross-linked in vivo with the 6-plex iqPIR individually, with randomized labeling. After cell lysis and protein extraction, iqPIR cross-linked samples were mixed in one final tube, followed by proteolytic digestion. (b) The multiplexed sample was then fractionated by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) and then by strong cation exchange (SCX). Cross-linked peptides were enriched using avidin beads. Samples were prepared for LC-MSn analysis. The data analysis and cross-link quantitation was performed as described by Chavez et al. . (c) Detailed 6-plex iqPIR qXL-MS pipeline with a representative cross-link. Fractions are separated by liquid chromatography and analyzed with high resolution MS/MS; MS1 spectrum highlighting the isotope envelope of the precursor ion, embedding all 6 cross-linked peptides; MS2 spectrum with highlighted fragment ions from peptides A (b/y ions in green) and B (b/y ions in purple), and isotope envelopes from released reporter ions and backbone peptides A and B, with the peaks colored according to the corresponding channel/drug.
